newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt militants say will ignore truce call.
newsitem.headline: Egypt militants say will ignore truce call.

text.p: The main Moslem militant group in Egypt has said that it will ignore a call by its imprisoned leaders to stop its military campaign against the government.
"We confirm...that we will continue our fight," said a statement signed by the Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), and received by Reuters on Sunday.

Six imprisoned Gama'a leaders have asked their followers to stop unilaterally all acts of violence. Their appeal was read at a military court on July 5 by Amin Abdul Alim, a defendant in the trial of 97 alleged Islamist militants.

"The Gama'a urges its brothers to stop military operations inside and outside Egypt and stop issuing all statements of incitement," he said. "This is a call from leaders of the Gama'a al-Islamiya at Tora prison."

He named them as Karam Mohamed Zuhdi, Nageh Ibrahim Abdullah, Abboud al-Zumur, Fouad el-Dualibi, Hamdi Abdul Rahman and Ali el-Sherif -- men imprisoned in connection with the assassination of president Anwar Sadat in 1981.

On July 6, Muntasser el-Zayyat, an Islamist lawyer known for his close contacts with the militants, told Reuters: "I confirm the statement is genuine, because Abdul Alim gave me signs...that he was speaking on behalf of the five."
The Gama'a statement on Sunday questioned the authenticity of the appeal, regarding it as a government bid to break up the group's unity.
"How can our brothers, who are being tried in this case (Abdul Alim), get in contact with their leaders in the prison? They have been in solitary confinement for years...," it said.
Another source close to the Gama'a said by telephone that Sunday's statement was authentic. "The latest statement represents the view of leaders of the Gama'a abroad," he said.
"The regime tried to shake the group's image, ...even suggesting that there was a break in the group's lines," he said, referring to the imprisoned leaders' appeal.
The Gama'a has been fighting the security forces since 1992 in a low-level guerrilla war largely confined to southern Egypt. More than 1,000 people have been killed in the conflict.
Yasser el-Sirry, an Islamist sentenced to death in Egypt and living in exile in Britain, told Reuters on Sunday the Gama'a had considered the leaders' appeal as a recommendation.
Police say they have broken the back of the military wing of the Gama'a through raids on its hideouts and steps to prevent the organisation receiving help from abroad.

The number of Gama'a attacks has declined sharply since the mid-1990s, when the militants were killing about one policeman a day. In Cairo the organisation tried to kill the prime minister, the interior minister and the information minister.
Gama's aim is to set up a strict Islamic state in Egypt.
